cards.front: Recall a key point about Rock Music of the 1960s and 1970s
cards.back: Power chords (root + fifth, no third) create a raw, powerful sound — they are ambiguous between major and minor, giving rock its aggressive character.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Rock Music of the 1960s and 1970s
cards.back: Drum kit in rock: kick drum (beats 1 and 3), snare (beats 2 and 4 = backbeat), hi-hat (subdivides the beat), crash cymbal (accents).

cards.front: Recall a key point about Rock Music of the 1960s and 1970s
cards.back: Studio production became a creative tool: automatic double-tracking (ADT) thickens vocal sound; reverb creates spatial depth; distortion adds harmonic richness.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Rock Music of the 1960s and 1970s
cards.back: Progressive rock expanded rock's structural scope: longer forms, classical influences, concept albums, complex time signatures and technical virtuosity.

cards.front: What should you know about music exam tips?
cards.back: Name guitar techniques precisely (palm mute, hammer-on, slide). Identify drum kit patterns (backbeat, fill). Explain studio production effects. Analyse structure (verse-chorus, intro-outro).

Students often make mistakes here. Wrong: Rock music is too simple to need musical analysis. Correct: Rock music uses sophisticated musical elements: specific guitar techniques (palm mute, hammer-on, pull-off, slide), complex drum patterns, layered textures, and innovative studio production. The exam expects you to analyse rock using the same musical vocabulary as any other genre.
Analyse a rock track from the 1960s or 1970s, identifying at least four specific instrumental techniques and explaining their contribution to the track's character.
